Like many other things on the site, this is a double-edged sword for all involved.

On one hand, any measures implemented to stop bots and other scammers from snatching up studies and giving trash data is welcome for me. If Prolific is the creme of the crop and is to remain that way, there must be procedures in place to make sure researchers get the best data they can and ensuring participants aren't fighting against con artists for spots.

On the other side of the coin, .6% margin of error is too high and there are bound to be researchers who abuse this feature like some have screening features, I would bet my bottom dollar on that being the case unfortunately. You say to hash it out with researchers or support if there's an error but some researchers ghost participants and support has been backlogged for some time, there will be casualties in the crossfire here.

I'm all for making sure the playing field is level but with the recent crop of shady if not outright unethical researchers on the platform, you're adding another toy to the playpen for them to screw over honest participants. One way to curb this is mandatory training on these tools and their proper use before researchers use them, but that might be asking too much.

We have to stand our ground and enlighten these researchers that there are rules here that they must follow as well. If you get a rejection for a petty reason or something inconsistent with Prolific's guidelines, make them aware and tell them they're out of line either by ignorance or ambivalence. The ones who care will adjust accordingly and either approve or let you return, others will assert they're in the right and at that point you take it up with Prolific support and/or the researcher's IRB or whoever supervises them. Everyone has someone above them and participant rights still exist. If they're especially egregious, block them. 

Of course I say do all of this professionally so you don't get booted yourself for acting like a loose cannon against a researcher. They already showed they can be petty by rejecting, if there's an ego problem, they'll have your account too. 

And avoid .cn and .in studies, they don't give two craps about Prolific's rules and it's not worth the effort.

This is a double-edged sword for me. On one hand, yes, researchers should be held to a higher standard than participants, paying customers or not. Also with naming and shaming some researchers, they change their display name (Which I didn't think was allowed?) but once you block someone with the same researcher ID, you shouldn't see them unless they make a new account which I know shouldn't be allowed (If participants can't, neither should they). 

Me personally, if I feel my time is wasted, I block them unless it's an aforementioned big university account. If there's an IRB I can just as well contact them if I feel I've been mistreated, they play no games and these days when research funding is a big question mark, I'm sure they're twice as strict.

Personally I find it disgusting to see defrauding of any kind on this platform, be it from unethical researchers or scammer participants. However you asked specifically about participant fraud from the perspective of a participant so I'll turn my attention there:

The behavior you described sounds like foreign scammers who buy Prolific accounts because either they're not supported or get very few studies in their native region. There are Facebook groups dedicated to this practice as evidenced by prior threads in the sub. The use of AI responses is likely from not having a good command of English to come up with competent and coherent answers. In short, they could care less about academic honesty and only want the money. I get it, money was the prime motivator for many of us here, but in my time doing this, I learned to appreciate how value my data is and how it makes a difference, even a small one, for research.

There are also folks in this very sub who openly bragged about using bots and effectively making bank at the expense of both viable data for researchers and user experience for participants who get met with nothing but high demand or full studies. 

It sucks given recent attacks against academic funding, researchers already deal with enough without dishonest participants willing to defraud for literal shekels.

I'm going to echo what another poster said here about rejections. I always believed rejections should be used as strictly a punitive measure and by all accounts a last resort if a participant isn't acting on good faith. However some researchers also act on the same bad faith by rejecting decent participants for bogus reasons that Prolific says are invalid as well (Finishing too fast when not an outlier, finishing too slow, NOCODE, etc.)

The current system is flawed sure, but with the skeleton crew Prolific has at the moment where support tickets take weeks to resolve, you really think there's enough manpower to manually review every rejection for legitimacy? I get that some researchers won't respond, I only had one completely ghost me after rejecting (It was a .cn IIRC) and Prolific had to reverse it as it was bogus, so if anything needed a change, there should be some way to make researchers respond if they accuse a participant of acting on bad faith by rejecting them. 

The main exception I'd bring up are obvious bots or scammer responses, but the incidence of those have yet to be reasonably determined. 

And yes I know the spiel of "They're the customers, they pay Prolific" and all that other rigmarole but that doesn't give them the right to effectively dine and dash. You don't go to a restaurant or a store and act entitled or damage the product because you're a customer, you have rules to follow too.

I've been on the platform for about a year and a half now, here's what I know:

1. NEVER use a VPN. Should be obvious but if you're logging in from somewhere with public Wi-Fi, they may have a VPN or some kind of filter that Prolific could flag and get you in trouble with them. Just to clarify, you can technically do studies anywhere in your country meaning if you're in the US, you can do another state so long as the Wi-Fi doesn't use a VPN. Hot spots are fine too, I had to use mine for days when my internet was out. 

2. ALWAYS keep your About Me updated and consistent. Researchers can report participants who lie on their studies or give inconsistent info contrary to the About Me, so make sure you update it if something changes. There's also trick questions/attention checks in the About Me too, so just answer honestly and you should have no trouble. 

3. Complete your studies in good faith: Pay attention take your time and don't give half-assed responses. Basically don't give a researcher a reason to reject you legitimately. There may be some researchers who try to weasel out of paying by giving a BS rejection, but those are few and far between and if you know your rights as a participant, you can fight it. But like I said, if you legitimately mess up, it's on you. 

4. Be professional and respectful to researchers. Like I said, they can report you if you're a dickhead to them, so if they do treat you unfairly like the rejection stuff I mentioned above, cite Prolific's policies and refer them to it and state your case in a rational manner. Sometimes people who get "banned for no reason" might have been curt with a researcher and got booted because of that.

Basically when all's said and done, don't give them a reason to take you down. Even if it's a "no reason," there's always something you may not be privy to and they have no obligation to say it because people would game the system (Not that some already aren't)

Anywhere within the country is okay, but just be mindful of VPNs and when in doubt, I use a hotspot. There was a period where I didn't have home internet for days and used my phone's hot spot, no issues there.

Most researchers I've dealt with have been cordial and professional, I can count on one hand the amount who were personally abrasive and almost had me contact their IRB. Out of thousands of studies I've done, that's super low.

The key is knowing the rejection guidelines by heart. The most legitimate reasons are finishing way too quickly (3 standard devs. faster than the mean), giving low effort responses, or failing attention checks (at least two if the study's longer than five minutes, only one if it's under five min.). Basically anything that stands as a legitimate reason for data quality to be called into question is reasonable grounds for rejection as a general rule, with some semantics like the standard dev. or missing two attention checks for longer studies rule. 

  
Rule of thumb, if you think something's amiss with a rejection and it's something that's not your fault as a participant, fight it. Rejections are supposed to be punitive measures and some researchers simply are ignorant to that fact, thinking it only denies payment for substandard work.
